newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Pre-handover-hangover worries HK before big party.
newsitem.headline: Pre-handover-hangover worries HK before big party.

text.p: Hong Kong's huge handover "party of the century" isn't until Monday but unsolved problems are giving the territory what one organiser called the 'mother of all headaches'.

First, outgoing colonial governor Chris Patten sent 4,000 invitation cards to a midnight transition ceremony, when Britain gives Hong Kong back to China, only to have the card design derided as "boring".
About a quarter of those invited have yet to respond for the June 30-July 1 historic milestone.

Then, hundreds of coaches and Mercedes-Benz limousines were laid on to transport guests to and from the festivities. Many invitees have not indicated whether they intend to take advantage of the offer.
With tight security at the handover site, it will be physically impossible for the guests to arrive by private vehicle -- even if all the roads in the area are finished.
Paving crews have been laying asphalt feverishly for weeks and teams of labourers are still working on their hands and knees to install brick sidewalks.
The city's new Convention and Exhibition Centre, where the actual handover will occur, looks impressive from across the harbour -- like a great bird about to take flight.
Up close once can see workmen scrambling night and day to get the building, including its roof, finished for the big event.
Heavy seasonal rains have complicated the construction process, just as they might dampen outdoor portions of the handover ceremony.
Working out a seating chart for 4,000 people would be a nightmare under the best of circumstances.
When those invited include heads of state, some not on the best of terms with each other, the job becomes tricky.
For instance, although they have a lot to talk about, placing Taiwan next to Beijing's delegation is generally held to be a bad idea.
A Hong Kong government protocol officer said on Tuesday the guests would probably be arranged in alphabetical order by nation.

Then there's the issue of combat troops from China's People's Liberation Army (PLA). In an apparent concession, Britain agreed to the entry of 509 soldiers three hours before the handover so they can be in place when the British leave their posts.
China is keen to have its troops visible at the handover as a sign of Beijing's renewed sovereignty over Hong Kong.
But there is a residue of anti-mainland feeling in Hong Knng as a result of the PLA's bloody 1989 crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Beijing's Tiananmen Square.
Observers say that with 500,000 people or more expected to line the harbour on the night of the handover any glimpse of Chinese troops could spark angry scenes.
Other demonstrations are planned to protest Beijing's decision to dump Hong Kong's existing, elected Legislation Council in favour of a hand-picked Provisional Legislature.
